title: Sing a new song (Psalm 96)
hook: let the fields be joyful and the trees sing
tomorrow: bless the Lord, O my soul

screen: `WARM AND DARK AND LOUD WITH HEARTBEATS.`

segments.voice: When did you last sing something for the first time? Not the chorus stuck in your head since the drive to work. Not the birthday song, or the hymn you could sing in your sleep. Something new in your own mouth. For most adults, it's been years, and there's comfort in the familiar. But the Psalms keep asking for something else. Again and again: sing a new song. And Psalm ninety-six doesn't stop at people. By the end, the fields, the sea and the trees are singing too.
screen: `THE SAME CHORUS, AGAIN.` → `WHEN DID YOU LAST SING SOMETHING NEW?` → `EVEN THE TREES JOIN IN.`

segments.voice: Psalm ninety-six opens, in the King James Bible: "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth." That phrase, a new song, turns up in several psalms, in the prophet Isaiah, and then twice in Revelation, the Bible's last book, where it's still being called new. So new here doesn't mean the latest hit. In the Psalms, a new song usually answers something new God has done: a rescue, a victory, a homecoming. Fresh mercy deserves fresh words. And this new song isn't for one nation. All the earth. The psalm tells the families of the peoples to give glory, and it says the gods of the nations are idols, but the Lord made the heavens. Then the song spreads beyond people altogether. "Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad; let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof. Let the field be joyful, and all that is therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice." Why are the trees so happy? The last verse says: "For he cometh, for he cometh to judge the earth." That sounds alarming, but listen to how it ends: "he shall judge the world with righteousness, and the people with his truth." In the Psalms, judgment often means setting things right. The trees cheer because justice is finally coming. And this psalm has a second home. Most of it appears again in First Chronicles, in the song sung when David brought the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem.
screen: `NEW SONG, FROM PSALMS TO REVELATION` · `FRESH MERCY, FRESH WORDS` · `THE FIELDS AND TREES REJOICE` · `JUDGMENT: THINGS SET RIGHT` · then, large: `O SING UNTO THE LORD A NEW SONG.`

segments.voice: Take the psalm's first line, O sing unto the Lord a new song, and give it a tune that didn't exist a minute ago: hum it first, then try the words; three notes, off key, it doesn't matter. If you'd rather, sing a hymn or a song you've never sung aloud before. If you pray, let it be your prayer; if you don't, let it be a small act of courage, and rest in the quiet after.
Chadash. Hebrew for new, the word behind Psalm ninety-six's call to sing a new song, with fresh words for fresh mercy, the fields and trees joining in.
Your line: a new song. Even the trees get a part. That's day four hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Psalm 96 is sung in many churches at Christmas and other feasts, and Christians often take its call to "sing a new song" as a reason to write new hymns and worship music for each generation.
